\title{\textcolor{navy}{\textbf{A Gold/Silver Hedge for a Dynamic SPY/TLT Frontier}}}
\author{Harness Research}
\date{\today}

\begin{document}

\begin{abstract}
This research note tests whether a liquid precious-metals sleeve improves a dynamic SPY/TLT allocation. The core sleeve holds SPY/TLT at 60/40, the metals sleeve holds GLD/SLV at 70/30, and the neutral reference assigns 80% to the core and 20% to metals. A causal volatility-gated rule moves along the rolling two-sleeve efficient frontier, with sinusoidal, linear, and quadratic five-session interpolation compared from January 2023 onward.

\medskip\noindent\textbf{Disclaimer.} This document is research software output, not investment
advice, and not evidence of future returns.
\end{abstract}

\tableofcontents

\section{Thesis and research design}\label{sec:design}

This note formalises an investment thesis as a testable mathematical object and evaluates it on
historical data. The pipeline is deliberately mechanical: a strategy maps the price history
available at time \(t\) to target weights (Section~\ref{sec:accounting}); a backtest converts those
weights into a net-of-cost return series; and every number quoted in the text is generated from
that series, not typed by hand (Sections~\ref{sec:performance}--\ref{sec:sizing} define the
estimators; Section~\ref{sec:results} reports them).

The research sample contains \NObs{} sessions from \StartDate{} to \EndDate{}. Trading costs are
charged at \CostBps{} basis points per unit of turnover. These assumptions are fixed before the
results are read, and they determine what the figures can and cannot show.

The key design rule is \emph{no look-ahead}: the weight vector applied to the return of session
\(t\) may depend only on information dated strictly before that return is realised. Formally, if
\(\mathcal F_{t-1}\) is the information set at the close of session \(t-1\), then
\begin{equation}
  w_t=g\!\left(\mathcal F_{t-1}\right),\qquad
  r^{\mathrm{strat}}_t=\sum_i w_{i,t}\,r_{i,t}-c\sum_i\lvert w_{i,t}-w^{\mathrm{drift}}_{i,t}\rvert,
  \label{eq:design-timing}
\end{equation}
where \(w^{\mathrm{drift}}_{i,t}\) is the previous target weight after drifting with the market and
\(c=\text{CostBps}/10^{4}\) is the proportional cost rate.

\subsection{Hypotheses}\label{sec:hypotheses}
\begin{itemize}
  \item[H1] The sinusoidal rule has a higher net Sharpe ratio than the static 80/20 core/metals reference.
  \item[H2] The static metals-hedged reference has a smaller maximum drawdown than unhedged static 60/40 SPY/TLT.
  \item[H3] The ranking of sine, linear, and quadratic interpolation changes across transaction-cost assumptions.
\end{itemize}


\section{Portfolio accounting}\label{sec:accounting}

\subsection{Currency conversion}

Let asset \(i\) be quoted in currency \(Q_i\) and let the account base currency be \(B\). If
\(X_t^{B,Q_i}\) denotes units of \(Q_i\) per one unit of \(B\), a native price \(P_{i,t}^{Q_i}\) has
base-currency value
\begin{equation}
  P_{i,t}^{B}=\frac{P_{i,t}^{Q_i}}{X_t^{B,Q_i}}.
  \label{eq:fx}
\end{equation}
Equivalently, with a direct multiplier \(Y_t^{Q_i,B}=\left(X_t^{B,Q_i}\right)^{-1}\) in units of
\(B\) per unit of \(Q_i\),
\begin{equation}
  P_{i,t}^{B}=P_{i,t}^{Q_i}\,Y_t^{Q_i,B}.
  \label{eq:fx-direct}
\end{equation}
Forward-filling an FX series onto an asset's trading dates is an alignment convention, not an
estimate of an unobserved intraday rate. When all assets share the base currency, both equations
are the identity.

\subsection{NAV and target weights}

With cash \(C_t\), position quantity \(q_{i,t}\), and base-currency price \(P_{i,t}^{B}\), net asset
value (NAV) is
\begin{equation}
  V_t=C_t+\sum_{i=1}^{m}q_{i,t}P_{i,t}^{B}.
  \label{eq:nav}
\end{equation}
For target weights \(w_i\ge 0\) satisfying \(\sum_i w_i\le 1\), the ideal target quantity is
\begin{equation}
  q_{i,t}^{\star}=\frac{w_i V_t}{P_{i,t}^{B}}.
  \label{eq:target-quantity}
\end{equation}
Equation~\eqref{eq:target-quantity} is the bridge between economic allocation and position size.
Unallocated weight, \(1-\sum_i w_i\), remains in cash and earns zero. The backtest uses fractional
quantities so that rounding does not obscure the mathematics.


\section{Returns, wealth, and performance}\label{sec:performance}

For a consistently adjusted price series \(P_t\), the one-period simple return is
\begin{equation}
  r_t=\frac{P_t}{P_{t-1}}-1,
  \label{eq:simple-return}
\end{equation}
and the log return is
\begin{equation}
  \ell_t=\log\!\left(\frac{P_t}{P_{t-1}}\right)=\log(1+r_t).
  \label{eq:log-return}
\end{equation}
Simple returns aggregate across simultaneously held assets; log returns add through time.

Starting from wealth \(V_0\), compounded wealth after \(T\) returns is
\begin{equation}
  V_T=V_0\prod_{t=1}^{T}(1+r_t).
  \label{eq:wealth}
\end{equation}
Total return and compound annual growth rate over \(Y\) calendar years are
\begin{equation}
  R_{\mathrm{tot}}=\frac{V_T}{V_0}-1,
  \qquad
  \mathrm{CAGR}=\left(1+R_{\mathrm{tot}}\right)^{1/Y}-1.
  \label{eq:cagr}
\end{equation}
Using \(A=252\) sessions per year and a zero risk-free rate, annualised volatility and the Sharpe
ratio are
\begin{equation}
  \widehat{\sigma}_{\mathrm{ann}}=\widehat{\sigma}_{r}\sqrt{A},
  \qquad
  \widehat{S}=\frac{\bar r}{\widehat{\sigma}_{r}}\sqrt{A}.
  \label{eq:sharpe}
\end{equation}
For the rolling graph, \(\bar r\) and \(\widehat\sigma_r\) are recomputed over a trailing window
using the sample standard deviation; the estimate is path-dependent and moves sharply when an
extreme observation enters or leaves the window.

Let \(M_t=\max_{0\le s\le t}V_s\) be the running high-water mark. Drawdown and maximum drawdown are
\begin{equation}
  D_t=\frac{V_t}{M_t}-1,
  \qquad
  D_{\max}=\min_{0\le t\le T}D_t.
  \label{eq:drawdown}
\end{equation}
These summaries describe one realised path. They do not quantify parameter uncertainty, multiple
testing, tail severity beyond the observed sample, or the probability of future loss.


\section{Estimation and uncertainty}\label{sec:estimation}

\subsection{Gaussian maximum likelihood}

For returns \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), assume as a working approximation that
\(x_j\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2)\). The log-likelihood, up to an additive
constant, is
\begin{equation}
  \mathcal L(\mu,\sigma^2)
  =-\frac{n}{2}\log(\sigma^2)-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{j=1}^{n}(x_j-\mu)^2.
  \label{eq:likelihood}
\end{equation}
Maximisation yields
\begin{equation}
  \widehat{\mu}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}x_j,
  \qquad
  \widehat{\sigma}^2=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}(x_j-\widehat{\mu})^2.
  \label{eq:mle}
\end{equation}
The divisor \(n\) is the maximum-likelihood convention, not the unbiased one. The estimated
standard error of the mean is
\begin{equation}
  \widehat{\se}(\widehat{\mu})=\frac{\widehat{\sigma}}{\sqrt n}.
  \label{eq:se}
\end{equation}
For the daily strategy returns of this study, \(\widehat\mu=\MuDaily{}\), \(\widehat\sigma^2=\VarDaily{}\)
and \(\widehat\se(\widehat\mu)=\MuDailySE{}\).
An estimated edge is only interesting relative to this error: the statistic
\(\widehat\mu/\widehat\se(\widehat\mu)\) is a \(t\)-type ratio, not a significance test, because
returns are neither established as Gaussian nor as independent.

\subsection{Stationary bootstrap for the Sharpe ratio}

Daily returns are serially dependent enough that the iid interval is unreliable. The stationary
bootstrap of Politis and Romano resamples blocks with geometric random length. With mean block
length \(1/p\), define the index sequence recursively: \(I_1\) is uniform on \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and
\begin{equation}
  I_{k+1}=
  \begin{cases}
    (I_k \bmod n)+1, & \text{with probability } 1-p,\\
    \text{uniform on }\{1,\ldots,n\}, & \text{with probability } p.
  \end{cases}
  \label{eq:stationary-bootstrap}
\end{equation}
For replication \(b=1,\ldots,B\) (here \(B=\NBoot{}\)), form \(x^{\star b}_k=x_{I_k}\) for \(k=1,\ldots,n\) and compute
\(\widehat S^{\star b}\) from Equation~\eqref{eq:sharpe}. The percentile interval for the Sharpe ratio is
\begin{equation}
  \left[\,\widehat S^{\star}_{(\alpha/2)},\ \widehat S^{\star}_{(1-\alpha/2)}\,\right],
  \label{eq:sharpe-ci}
\end{equation}
the empirical \(\alpha/2\) and \(1-\alpha/2\) quantiles of the replications. For this study the
interval is \([\SharpeCILow{},\ \SharpeCIHigh{}]\) around the point estimate \Sharpe{}. The interval
captures sampling noise under the resampling assumptions only; it does not correct for choosing the
strategy after seeing data.


\section{Position sizing}\label{sec:sizing}

For a small risky return \(R\) and fraction \(f\) of wealth invested, a second-order expansion of
expected log growth is
\begin{equation}
  \E[\log(1+fR)]\approx f\,\E[R]-\frac{f^2}{2}\E[R^2].
  \label{eq:log-growth}
\end{equation}
When the mean is small relative to volatility, \(\E[R^2]\approx\Var(R)\), and maximising over \(f\)
gives the familiar approximate optimiser
\begin{equation}
  f^{\star}\approx\frac{\E[R]}{\Var(R)}.
  \label{eq:kelly-approx}
\end{equation}
Because \(\E[R]\) and \(\Var(R)\) are estimated with error (Section~\ref{sec:estimation}), the
full-Kelly fraction is systematically too aggressive. A fractional-Kelly rule scales it by
\(\lambda\in(0,1]\) and imposes a cap \(f_{\max}\), after subtracting the per-trade cost \(c\):
\begin{equation}
  f=\min\!\left(f_{\max},\ \lambda\,\frac{\max(\widehat\mu-c,\,0)}{\widehat\sigma^{2}}\right).
  \label{eq:fractional-kelly}
\end{equation}
This is ``Kelly-style'', not an exact Kelly solution: return distributions are not established,
parameters are estimated, and the resulting weights are then constrained to
\(\sum_i w_i\le 1\) as in Section~\ref{sec:accounting}. Growth is concave in \(f\) around
\(f^\star\), so a fraction \(\lambda<1\) gives up a small amount of expected growth in exchange for
a substantially smaller variance and drawdown.

For this study, plugging the estimates of Section~\ref{sec:estimation} into
Equation~\eqref{eq:kelly-approx} gives an approximate full-Kelly fraction of \KellyFull{}; with
\(\lambda=\KellyFraction{}\) and cap \(f_{\max}=\KellyCap{}\), Equation~\eqref{eq:fractional-kelly}
gives \KellyFrac{}. A fraction above one would imply leverage; the strategy does not use these figures, which serve
only to show how fragile the full-Kelly value is given the standard error above.

\section{Thesis-specific model}\label{sec:thesis-math}

GLD seeks to reflect gold-bullion prices less trust expenses, while SLV seeks to track silver
bullion. They are liquid securities and imperfect commodity proxies, not direct delivery contracts.
To control estimation error, the four assets are reduced to two internally fixed sleeves. Their
returns are
\begin{equation}\label{eq:tm-sleeves}
 c_t=0.60r_{\mathrm{SPY},t}+0.40r_{\mathrm{TLT},t},
 \qquad
 m_t=0.70r_{\mathrm{GLD},t}+0.30r_{\mathrm{SLV},t}.
\end{equation}
For a metals allocation \(h\in[0.05,0.35]\), the four-asset weight vector is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:tm-weights}
 w(h)=\left(0.60(1-h),\ 0.40(1-h),\ 0.70h,\ 0.30h\right)^{\top}.
\end{equation}
The static hedged reference has \(h_0=0.20\), hence weights
\((0.48,0.32,0.14,0.06)^{\top}\).

Let \(x_t=(c_t,m_t)^{\top}\). Using at most \(L=126\) completed sessions, the rolling estimates
are
\begin{equation}\label{eq:tm-moments}
 \widehat\mu_t=252\,\overline x_t,
 \qquad
 \widehat\Sigma_t=252\,\widehat{\operatorname{Cov}}_t(x)+\epsilon I.
\end{equation}
The global minimum-variance metals share and the mean--variance growth anchor are
\begin{equation}\label{eq:tm-anchor}
 h_t^{\mathrm{gmv}}=\arg\min_h v(h)^{\top}\widehat\Sigma_t v(h),
 \quad
 h_t^{\star}=\arg\max_{h\in\mathcal F_t}
 \left\{v(h)^{\top}\widehat\mu_t-\frac{\gamma}{2}
 v(h)^{\top}\widehat\Sigma_t v(h)\right\},
 \quad v(h)=(1-h,h)^{\top},
\end{equation}
where \(\gamma=3\) and \(\mathcal F_t\) is the estimated efficient segment from the GMV point to
the higher-estimated-return endpoint.

The five-session compound-growth gap between the anchor and static hedged reference is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:tm-growth-gap}
 d_t=\prod_{j=0}^{4}\left(1+w(h_t^{\star})^{\top}r_{t-j}\right)
 -\prod_{j=0}^{4}\left(1+w(h_0)^{\top}r_{t-j}\right).
\end{equation}
If \(\widehat\sigma_{5,t}\) and \(\widehat\sigma_{21,t}\) are annualised volatilities of the
static hedged reference, the raw coordinate is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:tm-coordinate}
 q_t=\operatorname{clip}\!\left(
 \frac{\widehat\sigma_{5,t}/\widehat\sigma_{21,t}-1}{0.50},-1,1\right)
 \min\!\left\{\frac{|d_t|}{\widehat\sigma_{21,t}\sqrt{5/252}},1\right\}.
\end{equation}
Positive \(q_t\) moves toward the lower-risk point; negative \(q_t\) moves toward the frontier's
higher-risk endpoint. A zero growth gap leaves the allocation at the rolling anchor.

For interpolation type \(k\), the causal five-session coordinate is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:tm-interpolation}
 \widetilde q_t^{(k)}=\sum_{j=1}^{5}\kappa_j^{(k)}q_{t-5+j},
 \qquad
 \kappa_j^{(k)}=\frac{g_k(j)}{\sum_{\ell=1}^{5}g_k(\ell)},
\end{equation}
with \(g_{\mathrm{sine}}(j)=\sin(\pi j/10)\), \(g_{\mathrm{linear}}(j)=j\), and
\(g_{\mathrm{poly}}(j)=j^2\). The target formed after close \(t\) is applied to the return on
session \(t+1\).

\section{Trade and broker interpretation}\label{sec:broker-interpretation}

The latest completed-session target, dated \LatestModelDate{}, is \LatestSPY{} SPY,
\LatestTLT{} TLT, \LatestGLD{} GLD, and \LatestSLV{} SLV. Its smoothed coordinate is
\LatestModelCoordinate{}. These are model weights, not an executable recommendation. The supplied
IBKR planner checks for paper mode, reads current positions and base-currency prices, sizes
whole-share differences, and sets \texttt{transmit=False}; it never places an order.

\section{Evidence and limitations}\label{sec:limitations}

The figures show one realised path and are not evidence of dominance. The following caveats apply
to every paper produced by this pipeline, whatever the numbers say.

\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Sample length.} The sample has \NObs{} sessions (\StartDate{} to \EndDate{}). The
  standard error of a Sharpe ratio estimated from \(T\) years of data is roughly \(\sqrt{(1+S^2/2)/T}\),
  so short samples cannot distinguish skill from luck; see the interval
  \([\SharpeCILow{},\ \SharpeCIHigh{}]\).
  \item \textbf{Costs.} Costs are a proportional \CostBps{} basis points per unit of turnover.
  Real costs include spreads that widen in stress, market impact, commissions, financing, and
  taxes, none of which are modelled.
  \item \textbf{Overfitting and multiple testing.} The thesis was formulated with knowledge of
  history. Every parameter choice, ticker choice, and discarded variant increases the chance that
  the best-looking result is noise. The bootstrap interval does not account for this selection.
  \item \textbf{Model assumptions.} Gaussian and iid assumptions are working approximations.
  Financial returns are heteroskedastic, skewed, and heavy-tailed.
  \item \textbf{Data.} Adjusted closes are assumed correct and free of survivorship bias;
  the risk-free rate is taken as zero, and rankings can change with other choices.
  \item \textbf{No out-of-sample test.} Unless stated otherwise, no untouched holdout period was
  reserved.
\end{itemize}

\noindent\textbf{This document is not investment advice.} It is an automatically generated
research note; nothing in it has been validated for live capital, and past performance says little
about future returns.


\section*{Conclusion}

The chain of argument is mechanical: consistent prices give returns (Equation~\eqref{eq:simple-return});
weights that use only past information give a net-of-cost strategy return
(Equation~\eqref{eq:design-timing}); compounding gives wealth, growth, and drawdown
(Equations~\eqref{eq:wealth}--\eqref{eq:drawdown}); and estimation theory gives an honest statement
of uncertainty (Equation~\eqref{eq:sharpe-ci}). Over \StartDate{} to \EndDate{} the strategy
delivered a CAGR of \CAGR{} and a Sharpe ratio of \Sharpe{} against \BenchCAGR{} and \BenchSharpe{} for
the benchmark, with a maximum drawdown of \MaxDD{}. Given the limitations of
Section~\ref{sec:limitations}, these are hypotheses for further out-of-sample study, not
conclusions about the future.
